title: Ratio and scale factors
transcript: A ratio compares amounts measured in consistent units. To keep the same ratio, multiply or divide all the parts by the same factor. A proportion of the whole uses the sum of the ratio parts. A transfer changes the parts while leaving that whole fixed.

In AMC practice, look for scale drawings, recipes, or quantities mixed in the same proportion. Check that the units agree. In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, the ratio can change after something moves. Look for a total that stays constant.
One mixture uses two red beads for every five blue beads. Find the quantities for three identical batches. Which scale factor applies to each count?
Multiply the red count and the blue count by three. That preserves the comparison per batch. The new counts are six reds and fifteen blues. Dividing both by three recovers the original ratio.
On a one to one hundred drawing, a wall is four centimetres long. Find the actual wall length in metres. First decide what one centimetre on the drawing represents.

One centimetre represents one hundred centimetres. Multiply by four to get the real length in centimetres. There are one hundred centimetres in one metre. Divide the centimetre result by one hundred. The length is four metres. The factor from drawing to real length is the same before converting units.
A box initially has red and blue counters in ratio four to two. Move twelve from the red pile to the blue pile. The new ratio is two to four. How many counters are there in all?

The total stays the same. In both ratios there are six equal parts of that same total. Blue goes from two parts to four parts. That increase of two parts consists of exactly the twelve transferred counters. One part is six. Multiply by the full six parts. The box contains thirty-six counters.
The original piles have twenty-four and twelve. The transfer changes them to twelve and twenty-four. Reduce both pairs by the same part size. The two given ratios return, and the total is unchanged.

Multiplying just one ratio term changes the comparison. Apply the same scale factor to every term. When you need a fraction of the whole, add both ratio terms first. A three to five ratio gives three eighths for the first group.

Check that both sides use consistent units before calculating. Name one ratio part and write what it represents. For a change from one ratio to another, identify what stays fixed. Compare the same fraction of that fixed quantity.
